name: Maghreb sultanates (Marinids, Zayyanids, Wattasids, Saadis)
summary: Dynasties that ruled Morocco and western Algeria after the Almohads: the Marinids and Wattasids of Fez, the Zayyanids of Tlemcen, and the Saadis who defeated Portugal in 1578.

location.value: Morocco and western Algeria: the Marinids and Wattasids ruled from Fez, the Zayyanids from Tlemcen, and the Saadis from Marrakesh.

terrain.value: The Rif and Atlas mountains, fertile Atlantic plains, the Moulouya valley, and Saharan oases such as Sijilmasa and the Draa.

climate.value: Mediterranean on the coasts, cooler in the mountains, and hot and dry toward the Sahara.

resources.value: Grain, olives, wool, leather and horses; sugar cane in the Sous under the Saadis; gold and salt from Saharan trade.

disasters.value: The Black Death struck in 1348; droughts, locusts and famines also came often.

population.value: Perhaps a few million people across Morocco and western Algeria; no reliable count exists.

urbanisation.value: Fez (with the new royal city Fez el-Jdid, begun 1276), Marrakesh, Tlemcen, Meknes, Taza, Salé and Sijilmasa.

disease.value: Plague outbreaks, above all the Black Death (1347–51).

migration.value: Muslims and Jews from Spain arrived after 1492, and Moriscos expelled from Spain in 1609 settled in towns such as Salé and Tetouan.

economicBase.value: Farming and herding, crafts in towns such as Fez, and taxes on trans-Saharan and Mediterranean trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Trans-Saharan caravans through Sijilmasa and Tlemcen for gold and slaves; sea trade with Genoa, Venice, Aragon and later England.

wealth.value: Wealth from caravan trade; Ahmad al-Mansur, called “the Golden”, gained gold after conquering Songhai in 1591.

moneyAndTax.value: Gold dinars and square silver dirhams; Islamic taxes, tribute from tribes and customs on foreign merchants.

inequality.value: Rulers, ruling tribes and religious scholars above townspeople and farmers; Jews had protected but lower status.

governmentType.value: Dynastic sultanates backed by tribal armies; the Marinids and Zayyanids were Zenata Berbers, the Saadis claimed descent from the Prophet.

succession.value: Within the ruling family but often disputed; Wattasid viziers took power from the Marinids, and Saadi brothers fought after 1603.

institutions.value: Viziers, judges (qadis), the royal government (makhzen), tribal alliances, and madrasas for training scholars.

stability.value: Frequent wars between Fez and Tlemcen, with long Marinid sieges of Tlemcen in 1299–1307 and 1335–37.

eliteConflict.value: Rival dynasties, powerful viziers, Sufi holy men (marabouts) and princes competed for power.

armyAndTech.value: Tribal cavalry and Christian mercenaries under the Marinids; the Saadis used firearms and cannon from the 1500s.

majorWars.value: Battle of Alcácer Quibir (1578); Saadi conquest of Songhai (1591).

territoryChange.value: Portugal took Ceuta (1415) and Tangier (1471); Spain took Melilla (1497) and Oran (1509); Ottoman Algiers absorbed Tlemcen in 1554.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals of Castile, Portugal and the Hafsids; the Saadis balanced the Ottomans and traded with Elizabethan England.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; scholars at Fez continued work in law, astronomy and history.

scienceEducation.value: Madrasas in Fez and the al-Qarawiyyin mosque-university; Ibn Khaldun worked at Marinid and Zayyanid courts.

openness.value: Open to trade; closed to rival faiths at times.

communicationTransport.value: Caravan routes with camels and mules, roads between cities, and coastal shipping.

religion.value: Sunni Islam of the Maliki school, with growing Sufi brotherhoods; Jewish communities lived in town quarters (mellahs).

languageWriting.value: Arabic for religion, law and government; Berber languages widely spoken; Hebrew among Jewish communities.

artsArchitecture.value: Marinid madrasas such as the Bou Inania in Fez, with zellij tilework and carved plaster; the Saadi Tombs and El Badi Palace in Marrakesh.

socialStructure.value: Arab and Berber tribes, townspeople, Jews.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the ruler, to Islam and to tribe or city rather than a single nation.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; bread, porridge and beer or wine.

neighbours.value: Nasrid Granada, Castile and Portugal to the north, the Hafsids of Tunis to the east, and later the Ottomans and Songhai.

ideasReligions.value: Sufism and holy men (marabouts) grew powerful, and the Saadis used descent from the Prophet (sharifism) to claim rule.

colonisation.value: Lost coastal towns to Portugal and Spain.

riseSignals.value: The Zayyanids took Tlemcen in 1235, and the Marinids captured Marrakesh in 1269, ending the Almohads.

peakPeriod.value: The Marinid peak under Abu al-Hasan (1331–48), who briefly took Tunis in 1347, and Abu Inan (1348–58).

declineSignals.value: The Portuguese capture of Ceuta in 1415 began a long loss of coastal towns.

outcome.value: Followed by the Alaouite dynasty (Morocco) and Ottoman Algiers.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and charters; population figures are estimates.
